R05-B-01: A common complaint about relative poverty lines is that they confuse poverty with inequality. If a household counts as poor whenever its income falls below, say, half of the median, then a country in which everyone became twice as rich would have exactly as many poor people as before. Critics take this as a decisive objection: a measure that cannot register a general rise in living standards, they say, is measuring the spread of incomes and calling it hardship. The objection is tidy, and it is not wrong about the arithmetic. It is wrong, I think, about what poverty is. Being poor has never meant only lacking the calories and shelter needed to stay alive. It has meant being unable to do what one's neighbours take for granted: to send a child to school in clothes that will not draw mockery, to return a dinner invitation, to keep a telephone so that an employer can call. These requirements are set by the society one lives in, and they rise as that society grows richer. A family that could once manage without a refrigerator or a bank account cannot easily do so when shops, schools and employers assume that it has both. Relative lines track this moving threshold of participation, and that is exactly why their indifference to a uniform rise in incomes is not a defect. If everyone's income doubled, the cost of taking part in ordinary life would roughly double too. This does not mean that relative measures can stand alone. Their weakness shows most plainly in a recession. When median income falls, the line falls with it, and a household whose income has not changed may be counted as having escaped poverty while its circumstances are no better, and its anxieties perhaps worse. A measure that reports falling poverty in the middle of a slump will strike most people as perverse, and they will be right. Absolute lines, fixed in real terms at some past standard, have the opposite virtue: they register whether the poorest are gaining or losing ground in purchasing power, whatever is happening to everyone else. The sensible conclusion is not to choose between the two but to read them together, as answers to different questions. An absolute line asks whether the poor can buy more than they could before; a relative line asks whether they can still live as members of the society around them. A government that improves the first while the second worsens has achieved something real, but it has not abolished poverty, and it should not be allowed to claim that it has.
R05-B-02: Few proposals in development policy provoke as reliable a reaction as giving poor households money with no strings attached. The objection usually arrives before the argument has been heard: the money will be drunk, gambled or otherwise wasted. It is worth noticing how rarely this suspicion is applied to other recipients of public money: pensioners are not asked to show receipts, and a tax refund arrives without an accompanying lecture on how it ought to be spent. The worry is reserved for people whose poverty is taken, often without anyone saying so, as evidence that they cannot be trusted with choices. The suspicion has been tested more often than its persistence would suggest. Evaluations of cash programmes in a range of poor countries have generally found little sign that recipients increase their spending on alcohol or tobacco, and many have found the money going to food, school costs, livestock, tools and the repair of homes. This should not be surprising, since a household living close to the margin knows its own most pressing constraint far better than an official in a distant ministry, and the constraint differs from one family to the next: a roof for one, a debt for another, a sewing machine for a third. A transfer in kind, or one tied to a particular use, has to guess, and it guesses the same thing for everyone. None of this makes conditions pointless. Where the aim is a specific behaviour whose benefits fall partly on others, or arrive too late to weigh heavily with a hard-pressed parent, such as keeping a daughter in school or bringing an infant for vaccination, a condition can do work that cash alone may not. And in remote places where markets are thin, a sudden injection of money can push up the prices of the few goods available rather than raising what people can actually buy. These are genuine qualifications, and a careful designer of programmes will take them seriously; but they are reasons for attaching conditions in particular cases, argued on their merits, not grounds for a general presumption that the poor will misuse what they are given. The practical upshot is a reversal of the burden of proof. The default should be cash, and anyone proposing to restrict its use should have to show what the restriction achieves and what it costs, including the cost of monitoring and the quieter cost of telling adults that they are not trusted. Paternalism is sometimes justified, and there will be programmes in which the case for it can be made convincingly; it should not, however, be the starting assumption.
R05-B-03: For a period, small loans to the poor were spoken of as something close to a cure. The story was compelling: a woman borrows a modest sum, buys a second sewing machine or a stock of vegetables to sell, repays from her profits, borrows again, and climbs by degrees out of poverty. Lenders who reported repayment rates that conventional banks could only envy seemed to prove that the poor were creditworthy, and from creditworthiness it seemed a short step to prosperity. The step proved longer than advertised. When careful evaluations compared similar communities with and without access to microcredit, they tended to find effects that were real but modest. Some households started or expanded businesses; average incomes and consumption rose little, if at all; and the transformation of lives promised in the brochures was hard to find in the data. It would be easy to read this as a verdict that microcredit failed. That reading, I think, mistakes what was being tested. The original story assumed that most poor people are frustrated entrepreneurs held back only by a lack of capital. Many are not. They run tiny enterprises because steady wage work is unavailable, and given the choice many would take a factory job at a fixed wage over the uncertainties of a market stall. Seen in this light, the more interesting finding is how borrowers actually used their loans. A good deal of the money went not into enterprises but into managing life's lumpy expenses: a wedding, a hospital bill, school fees due all at once, a new roof before the rains. For households whose incomes arrive irregularly, the ability to turn a stream of small repayments into a single usable sum is genuinely valuable, even if it never shows up as a rise in average income. Microcredit, on this view, is less an engine of growth than a financial service, comparable to the savings and insurance that the better-off take for granted. This reframing is not a licence for complacency. Where lenders multiply and compete for the same clients, households can take one loan to repay another, and a service that smooths hardship can become a source of it. Nor should the modest average conceal a minority of borrowers, usually those who already ran established businesses, for whom credit made a larger difference. The lesson is not that small loans are worthless but that they should be judged as what they are, and regulated with that in mind, rather than against a promise they were never likely to keep.
R05-B-04: Among the ideas that have shaped thinking about growth and fairness, few have travelled as far as the proposal, first advanced in the middle of the twentieth century, that inequality traces an inverted U as an economy develops. In the early stages, the argument ran, inequality rises as some workers move from a poor and fairly equal agricultural sector into a richer and more unequal industrial one; later, as most of the workforce has made the move and the new urban classes gain education and political voice, inequality falls again. The idea was offered tentatively, on the strength of a handful of national histories, but it hardened over the following decades into something closer to a law. The mechanism at its core is sound as far as it goes. If a population is divided between two sectors with different average incomes, moving people from the lower to the higher will, by simple arithmetic, widen overall inequality for a time and then narrow it once the shift is largely complete. What does not follow is that this arithmetic governs the course of inequality in real economies, where it competes with many other forces. As data accumulated for more countries and longer periods, the curve proved elusive. Some economies grew rapidly while inequality stayed flat or fell; others saw inequality rise again after a long decline, a second upswing for which the original story had no room. The damage done by treating the curve as a law was not mainly to economic theory. It was to policy. If rising inequality is a natural stage of development that growth will itself reverse, then governments in poor countries can be told to tolerate it, and governments in rich ones can be assured that any widening is a passing disturbance. Both lessons encourage waiting. Yet in the historical episodes that did show a decline, the fall rarely arrived on its own. It came alongside the spread of public schooling, the growth of organised labour, progressive taxation and, in several cases, the destruction of concentrated wealth by war and inflation. A better reading treats the inverted U not as a path that development follows but as a record of what happened in some places when particular structural shifts met particular political choices. Read that way, the curve still teaches something, chiefly that the movement of people between sectors matters for how incomes are distributed. What it cannot do is assure a government that inequality will take care of itself.
R05-B-05: Debates about the informal economy, the vast realm of unregistered firms and unprotected work that employs a majority of workers in many poorer countries, tend to divide into two camps. One sees informality as exclusion. On this account, people sell vegetables on pavements or take casual work on building sites because the formal economy has too few jobs to absorb them; informality is a waiting room, and its occupants would leave if a door opened. The other camp sees informality as a choice. Registering a business, paying taxes and complying with labour law are costly, and for many firms the benefits of formality, such as access to the courts and to bank credit, are not worth the price. Informality, on this account, is a rational response to a state that asks much and offers little. Each camp marshals real evidence, and each tends to generalise from the cases that suit it. The exclusion view draws on the lives of the poorest informal workers, whose earnings are low, whose hours are long and who report that they would gladly take a salaried job. The choice view draws on a different population: owners of small but established workshops and trading firms who could register, who know what registration would involve and who have decided against it. Both groups are informal. They are not otherwise much alike, and an argument about which of them represents the informal economy is rather like an argument about whether the typical resident of a city is a banker or a street sweeper. The distinction matters most when governments decide to act. Programmes that cut the cost of registration, by reducing fees, merging permits or allowing firms to register online, are well designed for the second group and largely irrelevant to the first. A woman frying snacks at a bus stand is not informal because the registration form is long; she is informal because what she earns would not cover the obligations that formality brings, and because no employer has offered her anything better. For her, simplification changes nothing. Campaigns that instead treat informality as evasion and respond with fines and evictions fall hardest on precisely those who had the least choice. It would be wrong to conclude that the informal economy is merely a collection of unrelated cases. The groups are linked, since established informal firms often employ, supply or buy from the poorest workers, and conditions in one tier affect the other. But the links are a reason to design policy for each tier with the others in view, not a reason to pretend that one diagnosis fits all. The question to ask about any informal worker is not whether informality is chosen or imposed in general, but which of the two it is for that worker.
R05-B-06: A donor that pays for a new clinic likes to believe that it has paid for a clinic. Often it has not, or not in the sense it imagines. Suppose a government had already planned to build the clinic from its own revenue. When a donor offers to fund it, the government can accept, release the money it had set aside and spend it on something else entirely: a road, a pay rise for civil servants, an extra battalion. The clinic gets built either way. What the aid has really financed is whatever the government would otherwise have gone without, and the donor, which may never learn what that was, has had no say in choosing it. Economists call this fungibility, and once it has been seen it is hard to unsee. It implies that the earmark on a grant, the label saying that the money is for health or for schools, may tell us little about what the grant actually changes. Studies comparing donors' allocations with recipients' overall spending have often found that aid labelled for a sector raises spending in that sector by less than the amount given, though rarely by nothing. The lesson many have drawn is that donors are funding governments, not projects, whether or not they admit it. The lesson is right, but it is easy to overstate. Fungibility depends on the government having planned to do the thing anyway. Where a donor funds something the government would not have undertaken, a programme against a neglected disease, say, or a school in a district whose population carries no political weight, the money cannot be redirected in the same way, because there was no planned expenditure to release. Fungibility is also weaker when a government's budget is so stretched or so rigid that there is little slack to shift. And aid often brings more than money: technical staff, systems for buying supplies, and a degree of scrutiny that can change how a sector is run, effects that no accounting of shifted budget lines will capture. Nor is fungibility in itself a scandal. If a recipient government has sound priorities, the freedom to move money to where it is most needed is an advantage, and donors who insist on rigid earmarks may simply be paying for the comfort of a plaque. The difficulty arises where priorities are poor, because there the earmark offers protection only on paper. What follows is not that earmarking is useless but that donors cannot rely on it to do their thinking for them. The question that matters is less what a grant is labelled for than what kind of government receives it.
R05-B-07: Why are some countries rich and others poor? For several decades the question has been staged as a contest between two answers. One points to geography: to climate, soils, disease and distance from the sea, which shape what can be grown, how healthy workers are and how cheaply goods can be moved. The other points to institutions: to whether property is secure, contracts are enforced and rulers are constrained, which shape whether people find it worth their while to invest, innovate and trade. Each side has its favourite evidence, and each has scored points against the other. The institutional camp's strongest card is the observation that geography changes slowly while fortunes can change fast. Two halves of a peninsula with the same climate, the same soils and, until the middle of the twentieth century, a shared history can diverge dramatically within a couple of generations once they are placed under different political systems. Institutionalists have also pointed to a pattern among formerly colonised regions: some of those that were relatively densely settled and prosperous five centuries ago are relatively poor today, while some that were thinly populated then are rich now. Geography did not flip in the interval. What changed, the argument goes, were the institutions that colonisers imposed, extractive where there was wealth and labour to seize, more inclusive where settlers came to live. The geographers' reply is that these comparisons, however striking, do not dispose of their case. A landlocked country far from major markets pays more to export every tonne it produces, whatever its laws say, and a tropical region where malaria is endemic carries a burden of illness that good government can reduce but not abolish overnight. These are direct effects, and no amount of constitutional reform makes a mountain range easier to cross. Geographers add that the peninsula, however vivid, is a single case, and that a single case can show that institutions are capable of mattering without showing how much they usually matter across the wide run of countries. What both camps tend to overlook is how much of their contest is artificial. The reversal story itself, read carefully, is a story about geography working through institutions. Colonisers chose to settle or to extract partly according to how likely they were to survive the local diseases, and the soils of some regions suited crops that were profitable to grow with coerced labour on large estates. The institutions that resulted were, in this sense, partly geographical in origin, even if they later took on a life of their own. To ask, as statistical exercises often do, how much of the variation in income is due to geography and how much to institutions is to treat as rival causes what are frequently links in a single chain. The exercise can produce a number, but the number answers a question that the history does not pose. None of this restores geography as destiny. The institutionalists are right that the same land can support very different outcomes, and that a country is not condemned by its latitude. The point is rather that the question 'which matters more?' should give way to the question 'how did they combine here?', which has a different answer in different places and cannot be settled by a single coefficient. For one country the answer may lie largely in a coastline that made trade cheap long before anyone drafted a constitution; for another, in rules imposed by outsiders that outlived the conditions which first made them profitable.
R05-B-08: Income is the most convenient measure of how well people are doing, and convenience has a way of turning into authority. A figure for income per head can be compared across countries and decades, added up and divided, and reported to a decimal place. Yet what it measures is a means. People do not value income for its own sake but for what it allows them to do and to be: to be adequately nourished, to move about without danger, to read, to take part in the life of a community, to have some say in the decisions that shape their lives. The capability approach, as it has come to be called, proposes that development should be judged by these freedoms directly rather than by the resources that are supposed to produce them. The case for the shift rests on a simple observation with large consequences. The same income does not yield the same freedoms to everyone. A person who uses a wheelchair needs more resources than a neighbour to reach the same workplace; a pregnant woman needs more food than a man of the same age to be equally well nourished; a household in a cold climate must spend on heating what a household elsewhere can spend on anything it likes. Social arrangements matter as much as bodies and climates. Where custom keeps women from travelling alone, a rise in household income may leave a daughter's freedom to attend a distant college exactly where it was. Measures of income, by construction, are blind to these differences in the rate at which resources become lives. The standard objection is that the approach, whatever its philosophical appeal, cannot be made to work. Which capabilities count? How should being literate be weighed against being healthy, or political voice against freedom from hunger? Any answer, critics say, is either so vague as to be useless or, once written down as a definite list with definite weights, an imposition of some theorist's values on people who might rank their lives differently. A list drawn up in a university, they add, need not be the list that a farmer or a factory worker would draw up, and a framework that began by taking people's own lives seriously would then end by overruling their judgments about those lives. The objection is weaker than it looks, because it applies with equal force to the measure it is meant to defend. Income per head also aggregates very different things, and it also weights them. It weights them by market prices, which record what people with money are willing to pay, so that a luxury bought by the rich can count for more than a staple that the poor cannot afford. These are value judgments as well; they are simply made silently, by the market, rather than openly, by someone who must defend them. A framework that forces its users to state and argue for their weights has not introduced a new difficulty. It has exposed an old one. This does not mean that every attempt to turn capabilities into a single index succeeds. Composite scores that average a few indicators can reproduce the very problem the approach set out to solve, burying under one number the differences in conversion that made income misleading in the first place. The approach is at its strongest not as a rival ranking but as a discipline of attention: a way of asking, in any given place, which freedoms people lack and why, and of noticing when a rising average conceals a stagnant life.
